{{Short description|Geometrical GCD and LCM algorithm}}
[[File:Arithmetic-billiard-40-15.jpg|alt=The arithmetic billiard for the numbers 15 and 40.|thumb|The arithmetic billiard for the numbers 15 and 40: the [[greatest common divisor]] is 5, the point where the lines first meet on the y-axis, and the [[least common multiple]] is 120, the full length of the line in the x-axis.]]

In [[recreational mathematics]], '''arithmetic billiards''' provide a geometrical method to determine the [[least common multiple]] (LCM) and the [[greatest common divisor]] (GCD) of two [[Natural number|natural numbers]]. It makes use of reflections inside a rectangle that has sides with length of the two given numbers. This is a simple example of trajectory analysis used in [[dynamical billiards]].

Arithmetic billiards can be used to show how two numbers interact. Drawing squares within the rectangle of length and width of the two natural numbers allows a reader to learn more about the relationship between the two numbers. [[Coprime integers]] interact with every [[unit square]] within the rectangle.

== Properties==
[[File:Arithmetic-billiard-40-10.jpg|alt=The arithmetic billiard for the numbers 10 and 40.|thumb|The arithmetic billiard for the numbers 10 and 40.]]

Arithmetic billiards is a name given to the process of finding both the LCM and the GCD of two integers using a geometric method. It is named for its similarity to the movement of a [[billiard ball]].<ref name="Perucca"/>

To create an arithmetic billiard, a rectangle is drawn with a base of the larger number, and height of the smaller number. Beginning in the bottom-left corner at 45° angle, a path is drawn until it hits a side of the rectangle. Every time that the path meets the rectangle's side, it reflects with the same angle (the path makes either a left or a right 90° turn). Eventually (i.e., after a finite number of reflections) the path hits a corner and there it stops.<ref name="Perucca"/>

When the lines cross each other, the path becomes a [[zigzag]] consisting of one or more segments. Else, the path has self-intersections and consists of segments of various lengths in two orthogonal directions. In general, the path is the intersection of the rectangle with a grid of squares (oriented at 45° with respect to the rectangle's sides).<ref name="Perucca"/><ref name=recmaths>{{cite journal|author1=Antonella Perucca |author2=Joe Reguengo De Sousa |author3=Sebastiano Tronto |journal=Recreational Mathematics Magazine |title=Arithmetic billiards|date=2022 |volume=9 |issue=16 |pages=43–54|doi= 10.2478/rmm-2022-0003|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=lux>{{cite AV media|format=pdf|url=https://math.uni.lu/eml/assets/reports/2019/Carvalho-da-Veiga.pdf |title=Arithmetic Billiards|publisher=University of Luxembourg|first=Carvalho|last=da Veiga Bruno|date=Summer 2019}}</ref>

== Features ==
[[File:Arithmetic-billiard-8-3.jpg|alt=The arithmetic billiard for the numbers 3 and 8.|thumb|The arithmetic billiard for the numbers 3 and 8: the greatest common divisor is 1, the least common multiple is 24. A "bouncing points" where the line meets an edge. The number for each number can be measured by <math>(a/\operatorname{gcd}(a,b))-1</math>, so the total number for this rectangle is <math>(3/1)-1</math>+<math>(8/1)-1</math> or 10.]]

For a rectangle, shaped similar to a [[billiard table]], give <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> as the side lengths. This can be divided into <math>a\cdot b</math> unit squares. The ''least common multiple'' <math>\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)</math> is the number of unit squares crossed by the arithmetic billiard path or, equivalently, the length of the path divided by <math>\sqrt{2}</math>.<ref name="Perucca"/>

Suppose that none of the two side lengths divide the other. Then the first segment of the arithmetic billiard path contains the point of self-intersection that is closest to the starting point. The ''greatest common divisor'' <math>\gcd(a,b)</math> is the number of unit squares crossed by the first segment of the path up to that point of self-intersection. The path goes through each unit square if and only if <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are [[coprime integers]]—they have a GCD of 1.<ref name=lux/>

The ''number of bouncing points'' for the arithmetic billiard path on the two sides of length <math>a</math> equals <math>(a/\operatorname{gcd}(a,b))-1</math>, and similarly <math>(b/\operatorname{gcd}(a,b))-1</math> for the two sides of length <math>b</math>. In particular, if <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are coprime, then the total number of contact points between the path and the perimeter of the rectangle (i.e., the bouncing points plus starting and ending corner) equals <math>a+b</math>.<ref name=recmaths/><ref name=lux/>

The ''ending corner'' of the path is opposite the starting corner if and only if <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are exactly divisible by the same [[power of two]] (for example, if they are both odd), else it is one of the two adjacent corners, according to whether <math>a</math> or  <math>b</math> has more factors than <math>2</math> in its [[prime factorisation]]. The path is symmetric if the starting and the ending corner are opposite. The path is [[point symmetric]] in conjunction with the center of the rectangle, else it is symmetric with respect to the bisector of the side connecting the starting and the ending corner.<ref name=recmaths/><ref name=lux/>

The contact points between the arithmetic billiard path and the rectangle perimeter are evenly distributed: the distance along the perimeter (i.e., possibly going around the corner) between two such neighbouring points equals <math>2\gcd(a,b)</math>. Setting coordinates in the rectangle such that the starting point is <math>(0,0)</math> and the opposite corner is <math>(a,b)</math> means that any point on the arithmetic billiard path with integer coordinates has the property that the sum of the coordinates is even (the parity cannot change by moving along diagonals of unit squares). The points of self-intersection of the path, the bouncing points, and the starting and ending corner are exactly the points in the rectangle whose coordinates are multiples of <math>\gcd(a,b)</math> and are such that the sum of the coordinates is an even multiple of <math>\gcd(a,b)</math>.<ref name=recmaths/><ref name=lux/>

== Mirror images ==

[[File:Arithmetic-billiard-reflection.jpg|alt=Reflecting the billiard.|thumb|By reflecting the "billiard table" the path can be visualized as a straight line. In this example, the ratio of the two given numbers is 2/3.]]

Consider a square with side <math>\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)</math>. By displaying multiple copies of the original rectangle (with mirror symmetry), the arithmetic billiard path can be visualised as a diagonal of that square. In other words, one can think of reflecting the rectangle rather than the path segments.<ref name="Perucca"/> It is convenient to rescale the rectangle dividing <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> by their greatest common divisor, an operation that does not alter the path's [[geometry]] (e.g., the number of bouncing points).<ref name="Perucca"/> If the path is currently traversing one particular unit square (in a particular direction), then there is absolutely no doubt from which unit square and from which direction it originated.<ref name="Tanton" /><ref name="Perucca">{{cite magazine |url=https://plus.maths.org/content/arithmetic-billiards-0 |title=Arithmetic Billiards|last=Perucca |first=Antonella |date=April 24, 2018 |magazine=Plus Magazine |publisher=University of Cambridge |hdl=10993/35682|access-date= December 23, 2018}}</ref>

=== One generalisation ===

[[File:Arithmetic-billiard-35-14.jpg|alt=TODO.|thumb|A periodic path in the generalised arithmetic billiard with sides 35 and 14.]]

If one allows the starting point of the path to be any point in the rectangle with integer coordinates, then there are also periodic paths, unless the rectangle sides are coprime. The length of any periodic path equals <math>2\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\cdot \sqrt{2}</math>.<ref>{{cite web|title=Arithmetic billiards|url=https://orbilu.uni.lu/bitstream/10993/43834/1/Arithmetic-Billiards.pdf |page=2 |author1=Perucca, Antonella|author2=Reguengo de Sousa, Joe |author3=Toronto, Sebastiano}}</ref>

==Further information==
Both [[Hugo Steinhaus]] and [[Martin Gardner]] have discussed arithmetic billiards as [[Mathematical puzzle|mathematical puzzles]].<ref name="Steinhaus">{{cite book|title=Mathematical Snapshots|last1=Steinhaus|first1=Hugo|date=1999|publisher=Courier Corporation|isbn=0486409147|edition=Dover Recreational Math Series|page=63}}</ref><ref name="Gardner">{{cite book|title=Sixth Book of Mathematical Diversions from "Scientific American"|last1=Gardner|first1=Martin|date=1984|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=0226282503|pages=211–215}}</ref> Teachers sometimes use arithmetic billiards to show GCD and LCM. They are sometimes referred to by the name 'Paper Pool' due to a common version of billiards called [[pool (cue sports)|pool]].<ref name="NCTM">{{cite web|url=https://illuminations.nctm.org/lesson.aspx?id=1505|title=Paper Pool Game|website=NCTM Illuminations|publisher=National Council of Teachers of Mathematics|accessdate=10 January 2018|archive-date=10 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180210230338/http://illuminations.nctm.org/Lesson.aspx?id=1505|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://connectedmath.msu.edu/teacher-support/resources-for-teachers/unit-projects/comparing-and-scaling-paper-pool.aspx | title=Comparing and Scaling: Paper Pool - Connected Mathematics Project }}</ref> They have been used as a source of questions in mathematical circles.<ref name="Tanton">{{cite book|last1=Tanton|first1=James|title=Mathematical Galore! The First Five Years of the St. Mark's Institute of Mathematics|date=2012|publisher=The Mathematical Association of America|isbn=978-0883857762|pages=145–156}}</ref>
